title: Merlot around the world
subtitle: Softness and the Right Bank
objectives: Describe Merlot on Bordeaux's Right Bank

steps.title: The Right Bank
steps.body: Merlot is the most planted grape in Bordeaux. On the Right Bank, in Pomerol and Saint-Émilion, it leads the blend. Clay and limestone soils hold water and stay cool, suiting an early-ripening grape. The wines show plum, black cherry and a velvety texture; Pétrus, in Pomerol, is almost pure Merlot.

steps.title: Why Merlot suits cooler soils
steps.body: Merlot buds and ripens about one to two weeks before Cabernet Sauvignon. That lets it ripen on cool clay where Cabernet would struggle. But early budding brings frost risk, and its thin skin makes it sensitive to rot. In warm places it can overripen fast, losing freshness and turning jammy.

steps.prompt: Merlot ripens later than Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Not true. Merlot ripens one to two weeks earlier, which is why it suits cooler clay soils.

steps.title: Beyond Bordeaux
steps.body: Merlot is grown widely: in Italy, notably in Tuscany's Bolgheri and in Friuli; in Chile and California for soft, fruity reds; in Washington State for structured, fresh versions; and in New Zealand's Hawke's Bay. The 2004 film Sideways hurt its reputation in the United States, though great Merlot never went away.

steps.prompt: Which wine is famous for being made almost entirely from Merlot?
steps.explanation: Pétrus, in Pomerol, is almost pure Merlot. Margaux is Cabernet-led; Sassicaia is Cabernet-based; Vega Sicilia is Tempranillo-led.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Merlot leads the Right Bank blends of Pomerol and Saint-Émilion
It ripens early, suiting cool clay soils
It's grown widely, from Italy to Washington and New Zealand
